Niddesa 2.2 Rūpakaṇḍa (The Section on Form)
2.2.2. Mātikā 2.2.2.1. Ekaka:
Therein, what is all form (sabbaṃ rūpaṃ)?
The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements—
this is called all form.
All form is not a cause, is rootless, is dissociated from roots, is conditioned, is formed, is material, and is mundane.
It is associated with the taints, subject to the fetters, subject to the ties, subject to the floods, subject to the yokes, subject to the hindrances,

adhered to, subject to clinging, defiled, indeterminate, without an object, not mental concomitants, dissociated from consciousness, neither resultant nor producing resultant states, undefiled yet subject to defilement,
neither with applied thought and sustained thought, nor without applied thought and with sustained thought only, but without applied thought and without sustained thought.

It is not accompanied by rapture, not accompanied by pleasure, and not accompanied by equanimity; it is neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation, nor does it have a cause that is to be abandoned by vision or cultivation;
it leads neither to accumulation nor to diminution; it is neither of the trainee nor of the adept;
it is limited, belonging to the sense sphere, not belonging to the fine-material sphere, nor to the immaterial sphere; and it is included within the mundane.
It is not included [in the mundane], it is indeterminate, it does not lead to liberation, it has arisen, it is cognizable by the six consciousnesses, it is impermanent, and it is overcome by aging.
Thus is the summary of form by way of singlefold classification.
This is the first section.

2.2.2.3. The Triads.
The threefold inclusion of form:
That form which is internal is derived.
That form which is external is both derived and not derived.
That form which is internal is clung-to.
That form which is external is either clung-to or not clung-to.
That form which is internal is both clung-to and subject to clinging.
That form which is external is either both clung-to and subject to clinging, or not clung-to and subject to clinging.
That form which is internal is non-manifestive.
That form which is external is both manifestive and non-manifestive.
That form which is internal is impinging.
That form which is external: some of it is with resistance, some is without resistance.
That form which is internal: that is a faculty.
That form which is external: some of it is a faculty, some is not a faculty.
That form which is internal is not a great primary element.
That form which is external is both a great primary element and not a great primary element.
That form which is internal is not intimation.
That form which is external: some of it is intimation, some is non-intimation.
That form which is internal: it is not mind-originated.
That form which is external: some of it is mind-originated, some is not mind-originated.
That form which is internal is not co-existent with consciousness.
That form which is external: some is co-existent with consciousness, and some is not co-existent with consciousness.
That form which is internal does not follow after consciousness.
Of that external form, some conforms to the mind and some does not conform to the mind.
Of that internal form, it is gross.
Of that external form, some is gross and some is subtle.
That form which is internal is near.
That form which is external is both far and near.

2.2.2.4. The Tetrad.
The inclusion of material form is fourfold:
That material form which is derived is either clung-to or not clung-to.
That material form which is non-derived is either clung-to or not clung-to.
Of that form which is derived (*upādā*), some is clung-to and subject to clinging (*upādinnupādāniya*), and some is not clung-to but subject to clinging (*anupādinnupādāniya*).
Of that form which is not derived, some is clung-to and subject to clinging, and some is not clung-to but subject to clinging.
Of that form which is derived, some is with resistance (*sappaṭigha*), and some is without resistance (*appaṭigha*).
Of that form which is not derived, some is with resistance and some is without resistance.
Of that form which is derived, some is gross and some is subtle.
Of that form which is not derived, some is gross and some is subtle.
That form which is derived exists far away, exists near.
That form which is not derived exists far away, exists near.
That form which is clung-to exists visible, exists invisible.
That form which is not clung-to (anupādinna) is either visible (sanidassana) or invisible (anidassana).
That form which is clung-to (upādinna) is either impinging (sappaṭigha) or non-impinging (appaṭigha).
That form which is not clung-to is either impinging or non-impinging.
That form which is clung-to (upādinna) exists as the great primary elements (mahābhūta) and exists as what is not the great primary elements.
That form which is not clung-to exists as the great primary elements and exists as what is not the great primary elements.
That form which is clung-to exists as gross and exists as subtle.
That form which is not clung-to is either gross or subtle.
That form which is clung-to is either distant or near.
That form which is not clung-to is either distant or near.
Of that form which is acquired and subject to clinging, some is visible and some is invisible.
Of that form which is not acquired but subject to clinging, some is visible and some is invisible.
Of that form which is acquired and subject to clinging, some is impinging and some is non-impinging.
That form which is not clung to but is subject to clinging is either with resistance or without resistance.
That form which is both clung to and subject to clinging is either a great primary element or not a great primary element.
That form which is not clung to but is subject to clinging is either a great primary element or not a great primary element.
That form which is acquired and subject to clinging is both gross and subtle.
That form which is not acquired but subject to clinging is both gross and subtle.
That form which is acquired and subject to clinging is both distant and near.
That form which is not clung-to but is subject to clinging: some of that is distant, some is near.
That form which is with resistance: some of that is a faculty, some is not a faculty.
That form which is without resistance: some of that is a faculty, some is not a faculty.
That form which is with resistance: some of it consists of the great primary elements, some does not consist of the great primary elements.
That form which is without resistance: some of it consists of the great primary elements, some does not consist of the great primary elements.
That form which is a faculty: some of it is gross, some is subtle.
That form which is not a faculty is either gross or subtle.
That form which is a faculty is either distant or near.
That form which is not a faculty is also either distant or near.
That form which is a great primary element (mahābhūta) is both gross and subtle.
That form which is not a great primary element is both gross and subtle.
That form which is a great primary element is both distant and near.
That form which is not a great primary element exists far away and exists nearby.
[22] Form is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
Thus is the compendium of form by way of fourfold classification.
The Tetrad.

The fivefold classification of form.
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, and that form which is derived.
Thus is the compendium of form by way of fivefold division.
This is the pentad.

Form cognizable by the eye, form cognizable by the ear, form cognizable by the nose, form cognizable by the tongue, form cognizable by the body, and form cognizable by the mind.
Thus is the compendium of form by way of sixfold division.

2.2.2.8. The Section on Eights.
The eightfold classification of form:
There is form cognizable by the eye; form cognizable by the ear; form cognizable by the nose; form cognizable by the tongue; form cognizable by the body;
there is pleasant contact; there is painful contact; there is form cognizable by the mind-element;
and there is form cognizable by the mind-consciousness-element.
Thus is the compendium of form by way of eightfold classification.

2.2.2.9. The Nonad.
The inclusion of matter is ninefold:
the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the female-faculty, the male-faculty, the life-faculty, and that matter which is not a faculty.
Thus is the ninefold inclusion of matter.
The Ninth. 2.2.2.10.
The Tenfold: The Compendium of Form by way of ten aspects.

The eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the femininity faculty, the masculinity faculty, and the life faculty—there is material form that is a faculty which is impinging, and there is that which is non-impinging.
Thus is the compendium of material form by way of tenfold classification.
This is the decad.
2.2.2.11. The Group of Eleven The summary of material form by way of elevenfold division:

the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, the visible-form base, [the sound base, the odor base, the flavor base, the tangible-base, and the non-sensuous-material base].
The sense-sphere of sound, the sense-sphere of odor, the sense-sphere of flavor, the sense-sphere of the tangible, and that form which is non-demonstrable and non-reactive,
included within the sense-sphere of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*).
Thus is the compendium of form by way of elevenfold classification.
